description: Seeking teammates to build space-themed prototypes with NASA open data. I handle AI pipelines, data processing, Python coding and rapid prototyping. Looking for GIS/remote sensing, frontend UI, earth science or presentation skills. Let’s iterate fast and deliver polished demos.
summary: LunaMargin is an interactive lunar landing-site explorer for comparing locations and arrival dates under explicit mission constraints. It combines NASA LOLA terrain with NASA/JPL Horizons ephemerides to calculate continuous darkness, Earth-invisibility intervals, and simultaneous Sun-Earth visibility. Users inspect a selected point and eight neighbors, adjust mission duration and arrival limits, and compare alternatives without changing their thresholds. The tool reveals when a promising center hides a failing neighbor and when a nominally passing plan remains sensitive to finer calculations or tested perturbations. A linked 3D Moon, terrain map, timeline, and explanation cards make the results understandable. Saved missions and read-only shares preserve parameters, results, and versioned evidence for later review. LunaMargin supports early mission-concept discussions and lunar science education by making both the remaining margin and the limits of the evidence visible.
details:
LunaMargin addresses the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge through a practical question: does a promising location still meet the mission's limits when the arrival date or nearby position changes?

The tool supports early mission-concept design. Users rotate a 3D Moon, select a supported Connecting Ridge location, and enter a linked workspace. They specify arrival time in UTC, mission duration, maximum continuous darkness, maximum Earth-invisibility interval, minimum accumulated simultaneous visibility, and an arrival deadline. The map, nine-point view, timeline, and result explanations respond to the same selected position and time.

NASA LOLA elevation products provide 5 m local and 80 m regional terrain. The interactive baseline uses 30-minute ephemerides shared among nearby samples; selected audits use actual five-minute ephemerides and independent observer coordinates. The data pipeline constructs a separate terrain horizon for each sampled position. NASA/JPL Horizons supplies Sun and Earth directions. The algorithm compares each body's center elevation with the terrain horizon, interpolates visibility transitions between valid samples, and measures continuous gaps and overlapping visibility intervals. Nine positions spaced 25 m apart expose differences that a center-only assessment can miss.

Window search checks a six-hour arrival grid while preserving duration, thresholds, height, and the user's permitted arrival range. The complete mission must fit within available data. Users can prioritize the earliest feasible arrival or the greatest weakest margin within the inspected candidates. Up to three plans can be compared; differing conditions are displayed as tradeoffs rather than silently combined into one ranking.

Nominal feasibility and verification are shown separately. In the recorded case beginning 21 June 2027 at 12:00 UTC, with a seven-day duration, 2 m height, and 24/24/24-hour practice thresholds, ROI 1 and ROI 4 both nominally pass all nine samples. The combined five-minute and refined-geometry calculation leaves ROI 4's southwest sample with approximately 9.96 minutes of darkness margin. Adding a deterministic 0.02-degree angular stress changes its result to eight of nine passing samples. This stress test is reported separately from terrain uncertainty. Structured audits retain adverse results, missing checks, and the limited scope of official terrain-clone diagnostics.

The implementation uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, native WebGL, Node.js, and a Python geospatial pipeline. Vercel hosts the public interface and gateway; the existing Cloudflare Worker, D1 database, and R2 storage provide calculations and persistence. Named tasks preserve parameters, results, data checksums, and algorithm identity. Users can reopen original results, create read-only shares, and export HTML, CSV, or JSON evidence. Recalculation creates a separate result.

Current coverage includes three Connecting Ridge locations, December 2026 and March and June 2027, and a matched 2 m observer model. The default thresholds are declared practice assumptions. Outputs describe geometric visibility; electrical supply, ground-station communication links, and landing safety require additional models. The Moon's visual lighting is separate from scientific calculations.

LunaMargin's contribution is the connection between a decision, its weakest sampled constraint, and evidence that another person can inspect. It is intended to help concept teams and learners understand why alternatives differ. Automated workflow and consistency checks are documented; first-time-user testing and expert interviews remain pending.

OpenAI Codex assisted research, implementation, testing, interface graphics, documentation, and this submission. Development began before the event; the repository preserves the actual timeline. NASA has not reviewed or endorsed this independent project.

Some development tasks used coordinated AI agents. NASA LOLA products and NASA/JPL Horizons responses are external scientific inputs; derived horizons, visibility intervals, and margins are computed outputs. Practice assumptions and synthetic test fixtures are identified separately. The submission video is an edited presentation of actual interface captures with AI-assisted text and layout; it carries a visible SI disclosure throughout. No image-, video-, or audio-generation model was used. There is no synthetic narration or music. NASA imagery is credited separately.
